title: Ang 1294–1297: Kanara begins
hookLine: Guru Ram Das opens the night raga
tomorrow: a guy in the class group chat jokes about Sikhs. does she fire back?

lines: ONE A.M., A CALL FROM A STRANGER.
A NIGHT RAGA THAT STARTS GREEN.
cards: One in the morning. Simran's room is boxes and a mattress with no sheets. Her phone lights up: a video call from a number she doesn't know.
It's Hana, her new roommate, matched that afternoon, also awake, also buried in boxes, somewhere it's even later. They talk until both batteries complain.
Afterward, too wired to sleep, Simran opens the Granth to the next raga and finds something odd. Kanara is a raga for the night. And its very first line is about turning green.

teach.h: KANARA: A RAGA FOR THE NIGHT.
teach.b: Kanara begins on ang 1294 with Guru Ram Das, and tradition sings it at night.

In paraphrase, the first line: my mind has turned green, meeting the holy ones; I'm a sacrifice to them, and in their company I've crossed over. The word is hariaa: turned green, the way a dry plant does after water.
So why would a song for the dark start with leaves? Here's the puzzle solved.
In this hymn, what greens a mind isn't daylight at all. It's company, the sangat, people who turn you toward God. Leaves need the sun.
This mind needs people, and people can show up at one in the morning.
The night raga starts green because the company doesn't wait for dawn.
Here's something to tell a friend tonight: the Granth's night raga opens not with fear of the dark but with gratitude for the people in it.

Last week Simran stared at a housing form asking whether she wanted a roommate of her own faith, and left it open. Tonight the stranger on the screen asked about the steel bracelet on her wrist, her kara.
Simran explained, and Hana said she liked that it was something you keep on. Neither of them knows yet what they'll share. But Simran puts the phone down a little greener than she picked it up.

how: Ragis sing Kanara in kirtan, by tradition in the evening or at night; Guru Ram Das's hymns open the raga under the heading Mahala 4.

s: Kanara opens with a hymn about darkness and fear
its first line is a mind turning green, meeting the holy ones.
in this hymn, what greens the mind is company, not daylight
the sangat, people who turn you toward God, and they can show up at night.
sangat means only the people inside a gurdwara
it's the company of seekers, the people who turn you toward God, wherever they are.

games.q: you're new somewhere, and it's lonely after dark. with Kanara's first line in mind, what's the move?
o: find good company, even one person, and stay a while.
wait for morning; a night raga means nothing changes till dawn.
scroll until you're tired enough that it stops mattering.
games.why: Guru Ram Das's night raga opens with a mind turning green in good company. the green doesn't wait for daylight.

practice: Dim the light if you can, and let your eyes close. Bring to mind one person whose company leaves you greener than before, near or far, old friend or new.
Stay with their face for the sit, and on each in-breath, let the word green go through you once.
